articles.body: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle What I Built Every WordPress freelancer I know has a migration story, and none of them are happy. A client wants off their old host, or off WordPress entirely, and somebody has to move ten years of posts, pages, taxonomies, comments, and media into a new system without losing anything. The tooling is export buttons, importer plugins, and hope. The work is billable, dreaded, and one bad run away from a very long weekend. So I built the tool I watched people need for a decade in the hosting industry: migrateme.tech , an open-source, AI-assisted CMS migration toolkit whose defining feature is restraint. It is not a WordPress exit tool.

articles.title: 7 Nodejs Transactional Email Deliverability and Unsubscribe Practices for Payment Receipts in 2026
articles.excerpt: Nodejs transactional email deliverability practices for a payment receipt have one governing constraint: send only after settlement, while every unsubscribe, suppression, and bounce decision that coul…
articles.body: Nodejs transactional email deliverability practices for a payment receipt have one governing constraint: send only after settlement, while every unsubscribe, suppression, and bounce decision that could prevent or duplicate that send remains explainable later. The practical choice is to treat delivery as a ledger-adjacent workflow, not as a side effect of the payment request. Short answer: commit an immutable receipt intent with the settlement transition, dispatch it through an idempotent worker, separate transactional eligibility from marketing consent, and poll delivery outcomes into a durable suppression ledger when webhooks are unavailable. Warm new sending domains by increasing legitimate receipt traffic gradually, while keeping US and EU evidence partitions explicit.

articles.title: Three WebDAV Mount Mistakes That Will Ruin Your Day
articles.excerpt: WebDAV mount is the simplest way to make a remote server look like a local drive. But it's also the easiest way to lose data if you get the basics wrong. Here are three mistakes I've made personally.…
articles.body: WebDAV mount is the simplest way to make a remote server look like a local drive. But it's also the easiest way to lose data if you get the basics wrong. Here are three mistakes I've made personally. Don't be like me. Mistake 1: Assuming locks work automatically WebDAV has a locking mechanism. It prevents two people from editing the same file at the same time. Without locks, you can have a write race: machine A writes, machine B writes, machine A's write is silently lost. The problem: not all WebDAV clients honor locks. Some ignore them entirely. Some honor them but don't propagate them properly. Fix : When evaluating a mount client, check that it actually respects WebDAV locks. Test it: open the same file on two machines, edit on both, save both.

articles.title: Is an HTTP 402 Challenge Proof of Payment? No — Challenge vs. Settlement, With Live Receipts
articles.excerpt: Payment screenshots are circulating in the x402 ecosystem, and a lot of them show the same thing: an HTTP 402 response body. Here is the problem — a 402 challenge is not proof of payment. It is a pric…
articles.body: Payment screenshots are circulating in the x402 ecosystem, and a lot of them show the same thing: an HTTP 402 response body. Here is the problem — a 402 challenge is not proof of payment. It is a price quote. We proved it today on our own production endpoint. The free exhibit This afternoon (October 14, 2026, 22:01 UTC) we sent one unauthenticated request to our Verdict Protocol: POST https://verdict.scriptmasterlabs.com/decide (no payment header, empty JSON body) Back came HTTP 402 Payment Required with the full challenge: x402 v2, network eip155:8453 (Base), amount 250000 ($0.25 in atomic units), asset = USDC on Base, payTo = our settlement wallet. No wallet connected. No signature. No funds moved. Anyone can fetch that exact JSON right now — which is the point.

articles.title: Least-Privilege AWS IAM for Small Teams: Permission Boundaries, Access Analyzer, and Terraform
articles.excerpt: Small teams hit the same IAM wall. Either one person holds admin and becomes the bottleneck for every new Lambda role, or everyone gets AdministratorAccess "for now" and it never gets taken back. Neit…
articles.body: Small teams hit the same IAM wall. Either one person holds admin and becomes the bottleneck for every new Lambda role, or everyone gets AdministratorAccess "for now" and it never gets taken back. Neither scales. Permission boundaries offer a middle path: developers can create and manage their own roles, but no role they create can ever exceed a ceiling you define. Pair that with IAM Access Analyzer to generate policies from real usage and flag unused access, and you get least privilege without a dedicated security team. How permission boundaries work A permission boundary is a managed policy attached to a user or role that sets the maximum permissions it can have.

articles.title: Planetary genealogy: Milky Way worlds belong to 1 of 2 ‘families,’ scientists find
articles.excerpt: Scientists have performed a cosmic genealogy on planetary systems in the Milky Way, finding two distinct families that influence the evolution and fate of these systems.
articles.body: You can tell a lot about how a child will age by looking at their parents, and it turns out that this could be true for planetary systems, too. Scientists have performed cosmic genealogy on planetary systems in the Milky Way, finding two distinct families that influence the evolution and fate of these systems. The study team, led by researchers at the Italian National Institute for Astrophysics (INAF), studied 300 of the best-understood multiplanet systems of the over 1,000 that astronomers have discovered in the Milky Way. The team's research clarifies how the environments around infant stars directly affect planetary fates and, in turn, the survival of extrasolar planets, or exoplanets , that are potentially capable of hosting life.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 14, 1947: Test pilot Chuck Yeager breaks the sound barrier in the Bell X-1, the first X-plane
articles.excerpt: On Oct. 14, 1947, Chuck Yeager broke the sound barrier for the first time! Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Oct. 14, 1947, Chuck Yeager broke the sound barrier for the first time! Chuck Yeager was a test pilot for the U.S. Air Force who made history by flying an aircraft faster than the speed of sound. Yeager made his historic flight in a Bell X-1 rocket plane that he named "Glamorous Glennis" after his wife. Yeager had broken two ribs the night before when he fell off a horse, but that didn't stop him! His aircraft was dropped from a Boeing B-29 bomber before accelerating to a speed of Mach 1.07, which is about 821 mph (1,321 km/h). The speed of sound, Mach 1, is about 760 mph (1,223 km/h). USAF Capt. Charles E. Yeager (shown standing with the Bell X-1 supersonic rocket plane) became the first man to fly faster than the speed of sound in level flight on Oct. 14, 1947.
articles.author: Hanneke Weitering

articles.title: Life after the moon: Artemis II's Christina Koch steps down from active astronaut duty
articles.excerpt: Artemis II mission specialist Christina Koch will become NASA's acting deputy chief engineer on Nov. 1. All four Artemis II crewmates have now stepped away from active spaceflight duties.
articles.body: Don't expect any of the Artemis II moon astronauts to fly again soon. On Tuesday (Oct. 13), NASA announced that Artemis II mission specialist Christina Koch will become the agency’s acting deputy chief engineer, effective Nov. 1. "With this appointment, Koch will transition to management astronaut status and will no longer be eligible for future spaceflight assignments," NASA officials wrote in a statement on Tuesday . Her three Artemis II crewmates had already shared their next moves, none of which put another spaceflight in play in the near future. Mission commander Reid Wiseman and pilot Victor Glover , both of NASA, became "emeritus" astronauts last month, a role that seems to include planning, advising and mentoring duties but no flights into the final frontier.

articles.body: The truth is once again out there, as Disney & Hulu confirmed today that they have picked up a new "The X-Files" show for a full season. Described as a "reimagining" of the classic series, the project comes from Ryan Coogler, the acclaimed writer and director of "Creed", "Black Panther", and "Sinners", and will star Danielle Deadwyler and Himesh Patel. The show's premise will sound very familiar to fans of the original, as it centers on "two highly decorated but vastly different FBI agents who form an unlikely bond when they are assigned to a long-shuttered division devoted to cases involving unexplained phenomena." "I've loved 'The X-Files' for a long time, so getting the chance to write and direct the pilot has meant a great deal to me," said Coogler.

articles.title: Cosmic 'jellyfish' wows skywatchers after SpaceX launch | Space photo of the day for Oct. 14, 2026
articles.excerpt: A "jellyfish" in the early-morning sky created by SpaceX's launch of the CRS-35 cargo mission on Oct. 13, 2026.
articles.body: A "jellyfish" in the early-morning sky created by SpaceX's launch of the CRS-35 cargo mission on Oct. 13, 2026. (Image credit: SpaceX) Did you see a gigantic, glowing jellyfish in the night sky early on Tuesday morning (Oct. 13)? If so, it's not an alien invasion (sorry); it was SpaceX launching its latest mission to the International Space Station (ISS). What is it? Just before dawn on Tuesday (Oct. 13), a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket lifted off from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida, carrying to space a robotic Dragon capsule filled with thousands of pounds of cargo. The liftoff kicked off CRS-35, the 35th mission that SpaceX is flying to the ISS as part of the company's Commercial Resupply Services agreement with NASA.

articles.title: Anthropic warns small AI models could self-replicate through IoT devices
articles.excerpt: "Small weight-based replicators" could usher in a new generation of computer worms.
articles.body: AI company Anthropic is warning that advances in small AI models could soon usher in a new era of self-replicating malware that’s capable of infecting smart fridges, vacuum cleaners, and a wide range of other Internet of Things devices and is more resistant to takedown. By next year, smaller AI models may be able to autonomously self-replicate on all kinds of IoT devices, the company said. Eventually, the capability could enable computer worms, which propagate without requiring human interaction and are capable of infecting unfamiliar IoT devices. An experiment the company performed recently revealed significant challenges in bringing such an AI malware replicator to fruition, so the finding is necessarily tempered.
